passage:
"Aren't you coming to nets tomorrow?"
"No."
Bhupen's sister Payal leaned on the doorframe. "That was three days ago."
"It cost us the match. Everyone saw me drop it."
"You dropped one catch. You took two."
"I keep seeing it. When I close my eyes it's just the ball going through my hands."
"That hurts. But it's one moment in one match. It isn't you." Payal held out his gloves. "Coach asked about you. Nobody said a word against you in the team chat."
"Really?"
"Come and catch with me in the yard for ten minutes. Nobody else."

qa.q: How many catches did Bhupen take in the match?
qa.a: Bhupen took two catches.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling while replaying the dropped catch?
qa.a: Ashamed and shaken, seeing it every time he closed his eyes and believing everyone saw.

qa.q: What small step did Payal suggest?
qa.a: Ten minutes of catching in the yard with just Payal, with nobody else watching.

qa.q: How does Payal see the dropped catch differently from Bhupen?
qa.a: Payal sees it as one moment in one match, not a verdict on Bhupen.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying a visible error in a match for days and avoiding trying again, with a sibling's reassurance.

passage: In Class 9 I froze in the middle of the quiz finals, blurted the wrong answer loudly, and the whole hall laughed. For a week I replayed it. I stopped raising my hand, even when I knew the answers. I told myself I was just the kind of person who gets things wrong in public. Sarika ma'am, the quiz coach, kept me back after school. She did not say it was nothing. She said, "Tell me what happened. Only that." I described the question. "Yes, that one trips up a lot of people," she said. "Help me write the next round of questions." Slowly, I began to put my hand up again. - Chinmay

qa.q: What did Chinmay stop doing after the quiz finals?
qa.a: Chinmay stopped raising a hand, even when Chinmay knew the answers.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel about the mistake during that week?
qa.a: Ashamed, as if the error showed what kind of person Chinmay was.

qa.q: What helped Chinmay start trying again?
qa.a: Sarika ma'am listened without dismissing it and invited Chinmay to help write the next round of questions.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Chinmay's mistake?
qa.a: As an understandable slip on a tricky question that trips up many people, not proof of anything about Chinmay.

grounding: Shows a teenager who replays a visible error for days, avoids trying again and feels it defines them.

passage:
In the inter-school final in Chennai, Aadhya dropped a simple catch at mid-on. The batter went on to hit the winning runs.
For four days she replayed it. At night, in class, in the bus. The ball in the air, her hands, the thud on the grass, the groan from the stands. She stopped going to practice. When her friend Jyoti texted, "Nets at 5?", she replied, "Tired."
On Saturday, Jyoti came to her door with two cricket balls. "You're not tired. You're hiding."
Aadhya burst out, "Everyone saw. I'm the girl who lost the final."
"You're a girl who dropped one catch," Jyoti said. "You also took two wickets in the semi. Nobody remembers that because you don't let them."
They went to the park. Jyoti threw soft catches, then harder ones. Aadhya dropped the first, then caught nine in a row. On the walk home she almost smiled.

qa.q: Where was Aadhya fielding when she dropped the catch?
qa.a: At mid-on.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel in the days after the final?
qa.a: Aadhya felt ashamed and humiliated, replaying the drop and believing everyone saw her as the girl who lost the final.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that helped Aadhya try again?
qa.a: Jyoti named the hiding, reminded Aadhya of her two wickets in the semi and gave her easy catches first, so she could rebuild confidence.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see the dropped catch?
qa.a: Jyoti sees it as one mistake, not a verdict on Aadhya, and wants a friend back on the field.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who replays a visible error for days and avoids trying again, feeling it defines her whole self.

passage:
"Wasim, the debate club is tomorrow. You're coming?"
"No, Afreen."
"You haven't missed one all year."
"I'm not going back." He didn't look up from his phone.
Afreen sat on the arm of the sofa. "Is this about last Friday?"
"I forgot my whole second point. In front of everyone. I just stood there saying 'um.'"
"For how long?"
"Forever."
"About ten seconds, Nadia said."
"Felt like forever." He put the phone down. "Everyone thinks I'm the boy who froze."
"Everyone? Or you?"
He was quiet.
"Remember when I fell off the stage at the dance show? In Class Eight?"
"You rolled off. It was hilarious."
"I cried for a week. And then I danced again the next month, and now nobody remembers except you."
Wasim almost smiled.
"Go tomorrow. Just listen. You don't have to speak."
"…Just listen?"
"Just listen."

qa.q: How long did Nadia say Wasim was silent?
qa.a: About ten seconds, Nadia said.

qa.q: How does Wasim feel about the debate last Friday?
qa.a: Wasim feels ashamed and exposed, believing everyone now sees him as the boy who froze.

qa.q: What small step does Afreen suggest, and why might it work?
qa.a: Going tomorrow just to listen, because it lets Wasim return without the pressure of speaking.

qa.q: How does Afreen see Wasim's mistake?
qa.a: Afreen sees it as a small moment that others will forget, like Afreen's own fall at the dance show.

grounding: Shows a teenager who replays a visible error and avoids trying again, and a sibling who helps him see it as one moment, not a verdict.

passage:
In Class Nine, I went up to the board to solve an equation and wrote that two plus three was six. In the middle of algebra. The whole class burst out laughing. Even the teacher smiled.
I'm Shalini, and for about a month after that, I didn't raise my hand once. In every maths class I kept my head down and my pen moving. At night I'd lie in bed and hear the laugh again. It felt like the class had decided I was stupid, and maybe they were right.
My friend Yusuf noticed. One day after class he said, "You know you're the one who explained quadratics to me? I'd have failed without you."
I'd forgotten that.
A week later I raised my hand, heart thumping, to answer a small question. I got it right. Nobody laughed. Nobody even looked up.
It was one mistake. For a month, I'd treated it like my whole self.

qa.q: What did Shalini write on the board?
qa.a: Two plus three was six.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel in the month after the mistake?
qa.a: Shalini felt ashamed and small, hearing the laugh again at night and believing the class thought Shalini was stupid.

qa.q: What helped Shalini raise a hand again?
qa.a: Yusuf's reminder that Shalini had explained quadratics to him, which showed one error was not the whole picture.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have seen Shalini that month?
qa.a: Yusuf probably noticed with concern that Shalini had gone quiet, and wanted to remind Shalini of real strengths.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who replays one visible error for weeks and stops trying, as shame turns a single event into a verdict on the self.

passage:
Coach's notes, under-16 hockey, Wednesday.
Nirmala has not taken a single penalty corner in practice since Saturday's final, where her flick went wide and we lost 1–0. Today, when I called her name for the drill, she said she had a headache and sat on the bench retying the same lace. Her friend told me she has watched the match video "maybe twenty times" and keeps saying, "I'm the reason we lost."
After practice I sat next to her. I told her I missed two strokes in a state final at her age and still remember the smell of the grass. She almost smiled. I said one flick is one flick, not the whole player.
Next steps: tomorrow she takes five flicks at an empty goal, no keeper, only me watching. I've messaged her mother that it has been a hard week, so home knows to go gently.
Rukmini

qa.q: What was the result of Saturday's final?
qa.a: They lost 1–0 after Nirmala's flick went wide.

qa.q: What does Nirmala retying the same lace suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels ashamed and afraid of missing again, avoiding the drill because she sees herself as "the reason we lost".

qa.q: Why might five flicks at an empty goal help Nirmala?
qa.a: It lets her try again in a small, low-pressure way with only the coach watching, so one miss can stop feeling like a verdict on her.

qa.q: How does Rukmini see Nirmala's miss?
qa.a: Rukmini sees it as one flick, not the whole player, remembering missing two strokes in a state final at the same age.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying a visible error for days and avoiding trying again, and a coach helping her restart.
